Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 246 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 246 is located in central Alberta. The unit is adjacent to the border of 
Saskatchewan and is approximately 1336 km2. The habitat is dominated by agricultural land (pasture and 
cropland) interspersed with parkland vegetation.  
Previous aerial ungulate surveys conducted in these units have used the Modified Gassaway transect survey 
method with the most recent survey in 2004. Based on this survey, the white-tailed deer, mule deer, and moose 
population estimatehave ranged from 1661, 74, and 48, respectively.

Survey Method 
From January 9 to 11, 2019, a strip transect survey of WMU 246 was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 
kilometre (1 mile) intervals resulting in a 25% coverage (with 400 metre wide survey strip). Snow conditions were 
good. At each observation point, ungulates were counted by species, and when possible, classified by sex and 
age. Bucks were also classified by antler size as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’

(antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears).   
 
Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km2) of 
mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose by summing the total animals counted per transect ( ∑x) by total area 
searched (length of transects multiplied by 400 metre survey strip [∑z]). For a population estimate (unequal sized 
units, sampling without replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). A 
correction factor for detectability (estimated at 83%; Habib et al. 2012) can be applied to WTDE and MUDE density 
and population estimates in the Parkland for strip widths of 400 metre. A correction factor of 95% was applied for 
moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% confidence interval by multiplying the t statistic 
for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of 
the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N 
as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  Due to 
the variation in transect lengths, population estimates were determined by Jolly’s (1969) method for sampling 
unequal sized units without replacement (Krebs 2014). 
 
Because of the timing of this survey some antler drop is expected to have happened, resulting in a male -skewed 
unclassified portion of the population, in particular for mule and white-tailed deer.  
Results 
Out of 108 possible transects, a total of 27 transects were surveyed for a total effort of 328 km2. Non-ungulate 
species observed during the survey included coyotes, porcupines, red fox, and snowy owls.  
There were 486 white-tailed deer observed within 101 groups. Of the 486 white-tailed deer observed:  
 
 54 (11%) were bucks 
 267 (54%) were does 
 165 (34%) were fawns 
 6 (1%) were not classified 
 
Of the 54 bucks identified, 12 (22%) were classified as small, 17 (31%) medium, 5 (9%) large, and 20 (37%) were 
unclassified. The buck:doe ratio was 0.20 and the fawn:doe ratio was 0.62 (Table 1). The average white-tailed deer 
density was estimated at 1.76 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 2345 individuals (Table 
1). This corresponds to a white-tailed deer population split estimate of 261 bucks, 1288 does and 796 fawns. 
 
There were 77 mule deer observed within 13 groups. Of the 77 mule deer identifiedL  
 
 17 (22%) were bucks 
 35 (45%) were does 
 25 (32%) were fawns 
 0 (0%) were not classified 
 
Of the 17 bucks observed, 4 (24%) were classified as small, 5 (29) medium, 2 (12%) large and 6 (35%) were not 
classified. The buck:doe ratio was 0.49 and the fawn:doe ratio was 0.71 (Table 2).  The average mule deer density 
was estimated at 0.27 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 367 individuals (Table 2). This 
corresponds to a mule deer population split estimate of 81 bucks, 167 does and 119 fawns.  
 
There were 31 moose observed within 17 groups. Of the 31 moose identified: 
 5 (16%) were bulls 
 13 (41%) were cows 
 13 (41%) were calves 
 1 (3%) were not classified

The bull:cow ratio was 0.38 and the calf:cow ratio was 1.00 (Table 3). The average moose density was estimated 
at 0.10 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 137 (Table 3) and corresponds to moose 
population split estimate of 22 bulls, 57 cows and 57 calves.  
Lastly, there were 0 elk (both on and off transect) observed in the WMU.
